doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Jazz Education Network convention and the state of jazz
summary: He reflects on the Reno convention, jazz education and teaching today's kids, and calls himself very lucky.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: It did. Okay. You just returned from the Jazz Ed conference?
Yeah. Jazz network thing, in Reno.

Now when you’re out there and being surrounded with all those people and activity you might get one feeling about the state of jazz. When you come back here and you live here and you participate and you observe the jazz scene, do you get a different take on today’s state of jazz?

Well I wouldn’t say I get two different ones, they’re all part of one. It’s like not mirror images but it’s so inspiring going to those jazz conventions. I mean it’s just wonderful because you see what the music means to so many people who don’t live in New York or don’t live near the major metropolitan areas where there are jazz clubs. And these are the people that are keeping the flame alive in everywhere else in the country. And to see how the kids are so excited and all this kind of stuff, and they’re going to play their tune and they’re going to do this and they’re going to do that without realizing, and this kind of merges a little bit with your previous question, merging with American history. Every time you pick up an instrument to play jazz or to contemplate it, you’re part of some tradition, you’re following in footsteps, you know, defined by African-American geniuses. And you’re part of the story and it’s a great heritage. And it’s a heritage that you know is participated in by something that is for most of the time, fun, and playing an instrument and tapping your foot, and so it’s kind of profound. I mean it’s easy to look at jazz education or things like that less than charitably sometimes, when you realize that a large percentage of people who teach that never played in a band or never really had experience, I don’t find that very satisfying at the end of the day as not the proper way, but it’s how I look at it. I look at it, it’s all good. This is wonderful. These are people that love the music, we’ve got to support them and get to them however we can get to them. And a big problem with teaching, as I’m sure you know and we all know or as parents know, I’m not a parent, but that you can’t teach kids in 2019 assuming that they are like we were in 1976 or 1986 or as your students were in ’96 or ’06. It doesn’t work. And so consequently you know you’ve got to learn to adapt. And so that’s how I come back from the JEN convention in Reno, I heard some great music, I met some wonderful teachers, I met old friends, I made new friends, and I was just really pumped up just to see all these © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
people loving it. And I come back to New York and of course I’m very involved with the Jazz Museum and keeping an institution alive, and so yeah, it’s all part of one big picture.

I don’t have a summation kind of thing, but I’m just again going back to something I wanted to say was I’m probably the luckiest person. You know some people say well there’s luck but there’s also this and that and being in the position to have luck or something like that. Nonetheless I am among the luckiest people that you’re ever going to interview.
